Agent skills · handbook

Palette as an agent skill

Palette builds real PowerPoint decks from an editable plan. It cannot run inside an agent sandbox — it needs Node, LibreOffice, Poppler and a model roster. So the skill is not a copy of Palette: it is instructions for driving its HTTP API, plus a client whose only dependency is httpx. This is how that skill is built, released, kept current, consumed, and verified.

IBM/project-palette @ palette_skill cuga-project/cuga-agent @ palette

01What the skill is

A folder an agent opens when a task matches it — and a boundary decision.

A skill is a SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter plus whatever files the workflow needs. The host reads only the one-line description into the model's prompt; the body costs nothing until the model asks for it by name. That economy is the point — you can ship twenty capabilities without paying for twenty playbooks on every message.

The description is the whole routing decision. If it does not contain the words a user would actually say, the skill is never opened, however good the body is.

Why Palette is split this way

Agent side Sandbox Reads SKILL.md, runs palette-skill deck, writes ./deck/. Restricted writes, no heavy toolchain.
Boundary HTTP contract The only coupling. Palette's pipeline can be rewritten without the skill noticing.
Server side Palette Crafter → designer + coder → geometry repair. Node, LibreOffice, Poppler, IBM Plex, the model roster.

Two copies of a finished deck therefore exist, and that is by design rather than by accident: the server renders into its own workspace, and the client downloads the result over HTTP into the sandbox. When a slide looks wrong, the server copy holds the extras worth reading — deck.pdf, deck.json, output_js/, raw model predictions.

One command, not a sequence

Everything an agent needs for a deck is palette-skill deck. It owns the thread id, the plan file, the polling and the download, and it is idempotent — calling it again resumes. That shape exists for a specific reason, covered in §7.

the whole agent-side workflow
palette-skill deck --request "Q3 sales review deck" --dest ./deck --max-seconds 100
palette-skill deck --dest ./deck --max-seconds 100   # repeat until "done": true

Completion is not the model's to assert. Each result carries verified, computed by stat-ing the filesystem — the .pptx exists, is over 20 KB, and the preview PNGs are on disk.

02Building it

Generated from the server's own code, so the two cannot drift apart quietly.

SKILL.md is not hand-maintained prose about an API somewhere else. Its volatile parts are fenced regions rendered from the code that defines them. Everything outside a fence is authored by hand and never touched.

RegionRendered fromWhy it is generated
executionhosts.pyTool names and step limits differ per host
pollinghosts.pyThe poll window must fit the host's step budget
deliveryhosts.py"Where is my deck" has a different answer per host
unreachablecontract.pyLocal vs remote deployments need opposite advice
defaultscontract.pyBase URL, auth env var, terminal stages
endpointscontract.pyThe API table, with CLI and Python per route
modelsconfig.pyThe model menus the server will actually accept
examplesconfig.pyCurated plans, intersected with what is on disk
build and verify
make skill-build    # regenerate payload/*.md
make skill-check    # exit 1 if a region is stale
make skill-test     # assert the contract still matches app.py
make skill          # both checks — run after every Palette change, ~1s
The guard runs itself. make hooks installs a pre-commit hook that runs make skill whenever palette_skill/, app.py, config.py, session.py, requirements.txt or pyproject.toml is staged. Add a route without updating the contract and the commit is refused with the fix printed.

Installing into an agent

make skill-install CUGA=<path>
<agent>/.cuga/skills/palette/
├── SKILL.md                                     what the agent is told
├── reference.md                                 loaded on demand
├── vendor/palette_skill-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl  the client, httpx-only
└── .palette-skill.json                          host, version, commit, per-file hashes

The vendored wheel is what lets the agent install the client offline — no git access, no registry auth. The manifest is how make skill-status reports which side moved: it holds a client_fingerprint over the client sources plus a hash per markdown file, so drift detection needs no version discipline at all.

03Releasing it

For consumers who have no Palette checkout. Two modes, deliberately different.

mode one
Local build

Your own testing. Overwrites freely, no ceremony. This is the dev loop and needs no version.

make release
mode two
A real release

Anything someone else will rely on. Writes __version__, and turns on three guards.

make release VERSION=0.2.0
git commit -am 'release 0.2.0'
git tag v0.2.0
Why VERSION changes the rules. The version is not metadata — it is in every artifact's filename. Ship two different builds as 0.1.0 and dist/ overwrites silently, the recipient cannot tell them apart, and the manifest check that would catch it ("package version moved") can never fire, because both sides read 0.1.0.

The three guards

each refuses before anything is written
$ make release VERSION=bad
version must look like 1.2.3, got 'bad'

$ make release VERSION=0.2.0        # with uncommitted work
working tree is dirty — a released artifact records a commit
that would not describe its contents.

$ make release VERSION=0.2.0        # built once already
0.2.0 is already built: palette-skill-0.2.0-cuga.tar.gz
Bump VERSION, or delete those files if you are certain they were never shared.

Format is checked first — cheapest, and a typo should not be withheld until you have committed for unrelated reasons.

What comes out

ArtifactFor
palette_skill-<v>-py3-none-any.whlPyPI, or a direct pip install
palette-skill-<v>-cuga.tar.gzdrop into a CUGA skills root
palette-skill-<v>-claude-code.tar.gzdrop into ~/.claude/skills/
palette-skill-<v>-generic.tar.gzany other host

Each tarball is a complete skill folder rendered for that host — markdown, the client wheel, a manifest. Roughly 80 KB, no network, no build step, no Palette source required. Untar into a skills root and you are done, exactly like a skills.sh install.

Pinning a deployment

consumers then need no environment at all
make release VERSION=0.2.0 BASE_URL=https://palette.example.cloud

A pinned artifact also drops local advice: it will not tell an agent to run palette-skill serve ensure, because that would start a second, local Palette with none of the user's data. Pinning 127.0.0.1 is still local and keeps it. $PALETTE_URL overrides a pin either way, so pinning is a default rather than a commitment.

A release is pinned to a Palette version. The model menus and example plans are rendered from that checkout's config.py and then frozen — a skill advertising palette-qwen-32b has to ship with a server that serves it. So the artifact version tracks Palette, not the client.

04Keeping it current

Most changes need a reinstall, not a release.

LoopCommandNeeds a version?
Dev — you and your agent, one machine make skill-install CUGA=… No — drift detection is hash-based
Ship — anyone without a checkout make release VERSION=X.Y.Z Yes

Does a given change even touch the skill?

Don't work it out by hand — make skill answers it in about a second. Roughly:

ChangedSkill affected?
contract.py, client.py, cli.py, hosts.py, payload/ Yes — it is the skill
app.py routes or request models Yes — the contract test fails until you update it
config.py model roster or example plans Yes — generated regions re-render
renderer, session internals, the web UI Usually not — the HTTP contract is the only coupling

Checking what an agent actually has

which side moved?
make skill-status CUGA=../cuga-agent
palette skill at …/.cuga/skills/palette is in sync (v0.1.0, host cuga, commit c136b221a)
One stale copy hides from both repos. The agent installs the client into a venv inside its sandbox — on CUGA that is /tmp/.venv, shared across threads. A stale client there keeps running old code after you have installed new code, and nothing in either checkout will tell you. rm -rf /tmp/.venv is part of a full reset for exactly this reason.

05Using it — CUGA and Claude Code

One skill, rendered per host — and how to test each. The differences are not cosmetic.

Almost all of SKILL.md describes a service and is true anywhere. What is not portable is how an agent executes anything: the tool it shells out with, whether it may import the client in-process, how long a single step may run, and where a finished file surfaces for the user. Those come from a host profile.

HostShell toolPoll windowInline Python?Where the deck surfaces
CUGArun_command100s No — code blocks run under an import allowlist with no httpx The Files panel for that conversation
Claude CodeBash240s Yes The user's own filesystem — the path is the answer
Genericyour shell tool25s Yes Path only — nothing assumed about the host
The poll window is load-bearing, not a detail. It decides how many steps a deck costs, and that is what runs out first. A ten-minute build is twenty-odd polls at 25s and six at 100s — and an agent abandons the twenty long before any step limit is reached. Claude Code's Bash allows ten minutes, so one call can cover most of a build.

CUGA

cuga start demo_palette starts a supervisor agent — a Deck Builder rather than a generic skills demo. The preset raises two settings on your behalf, both with setdefault so an explicit env var still wins:

SettingDefaultPresetWhy
sandbox_execution_timeout30s120s Each bounded poll is one step. At 30s a long build is twenty-odd steps, and agents give up around step 40 of 100 — with the build finishing on the server and nobody collecting it.
cuga_lite_nl_auto_continuefalsetrue Mid-build the model often writes a progress note as prose with no code. That reads as a finished answer and ends the run.

The skill's CUGA profile polls at 100s to fit inside the 120s step; a test keeps the two matched.

Claude Code

Same skill, different rendering. Untar the claude-code tarball into ~/.claude/skills/ and it is discovered like any other. The generated execution section names Bash, Read, Write rather than CUGA's tools, offers the Python API directly (no import allowlist to work around), and omits CUGA's step-limit warnings — Claude Code does not cap a step tightly enough for them to matter. It also drops the Files-panel guidance, because there is no such panel and the absolute path is the whole answer.

Not overfitted. Adding a host means adding a profile to hosts.py — not forking the skill. Tests assert that CUGA's tarball never leaks the string Bash, that Claude Code's never leaks run_command, and that each ships its own poll window.

Testing it in Claude Code, end to end

Claude Code scans ~/.claude/skills/ itself, so installing is the whole setup. Run the installer from the Palette checkout — outside one there is no wheel to vendor and you get a skill folder with an empty vendor/.

install, then just ask
cd ~/…/project-palette
.venv/bin/python -m palette_skill.install --host claude-code
palette-skill serve ensure

# then, in any Claude Code session:
#   "build me a deck about vector databases for backend engineers"

Four things to watch, in order:

  1. It loads the skill rather than reaching for python-pptx. That routing decision comes from the description: line alone.
  2. It installs the client from the vendored wheel under ~/.claude/skills/palette/vendor/.
  3. It polls at --max-seconds 240, not 25. Seeing 25 means the installed skill is stale or was rendered for another host.
  4. It reports an absolute pptx_path and does not mention a Files panel — there isn't one here, and the path is the whole answer.
Installing for one host does not disturb another. install snapshots payload/ and restores it, so a --host claude-code install leaves the checkout and any CUGA install exactly as they were. That was not true until it was tested: the first Claude Code install left the repo rendered for Claude Code, and make skill-check began failing for no visible reason.

Which server is it talking to?

The client resolves $PALETTE_URL, then contract.DEFAULT_BASE_URL — which is http://127.0.0.1:18814. Local. A deployed instance is the intended default and is noted as such in contract.py, but no URL is pinned there yet, so nothing silently talks to the wrong host.

Don't reason about it — ask the log. The thread id is in .palette-deck.json:

who served this deck?
palette-skill health                                # what the client resolved
grep -l <thread-id> ~/.local/state/palette/workspace/*/session.log   # a match = served locally

# against a deployment instead — everything else is unchanged
PALETTE_URL=https://palette.example.cloud palette-skill health

Reading the result

When verified is true the agent is told to report, in order: the slide count and title, the absolute pptx_path — never the relative pptx, which names a working directory the user has never seen — and, on hosts that have one, that the deck is already downloadable from the UI.

06What testing means

Nine tiers, ordered by what they need. Stop wherever your environment stops.

TierNeedsAnswers
1nothingDoes the skill still describe this server?
2nothingDo the drift guards actually fire when you break something?
3Node, LibreOffice, PopplerCan Palette run here at all?
4an agent checkoutDoes the host discover and load it?
5+ Palette runningDoes the sandbox reach the server?
6+ LLM credentialsDoes a model pick the skill unprompted?
7+ a RITS keyDoes markdown become a real .pptx?
8all of the aboveDoes it work for a person, by hand?
9nothingCan someone with no checkout install the release?

Tier 2 is worth doing once

So you trust the guard rather than taking its word. Add a route to app.py and watch make skill-test name it; add a model to config.py and watch make skill-check call the payload stale; stage a change and watch the pre-commit hook refuse the commit.

Tier 7 asserts on the artifact, not the transcript

A long agent run gets context-summarised, which erases the very lines a transcript check would look for. So the tests open the .pptx: a valid OOXML package, the expected number of slide parts, a preview PNG per slide, a minimum file size — and IBM Plex in the slide XML. Palette's renderer forces that typeface and substitutes Calibri for anything else, so a deck hand-written with pptxgenjs defaults cannot carry it. It is provenance that cannot be summarised away.

Three routes in, matching how people actually arrive at a deck:

RoutePrompt shapeWhy it exists
Aa plan already in Palette's formatfast path, Stage 2 only
Braw unstructured notesforces Stage 1 first
C"Draft a plan for a Q3 sales review, show it to me, then build it"the regression test — see below
Route C is the one that finds things. A and B name the stage and say "poll until the build finishes"; under that much instruction the agent cannot fail the way it fails in the wild. C says what a person says. Every skill bug found so far came from a prompt shaped like C — none was caught by a unit test.

Route C also asserts that .palette-deck.json exists with "stage": "done". That file is written by palette-skill deck and by nothing else, so its absence proves the agent hand-drove the sequence — which is how a deck goes missing while being reported as built.

Verifying a deck by hand

three independent signals — believe the files, not the chat
# 1. the orchestrator ran (written by `palette-skill deck`, nothing else)
cat cuga_workspace/*/deck/.palette-deck.json

# 2. one session carried both stages
grep -E "draft_async|build_async" ~/.local/state/palette/workspace/*/session.log | tail -2

# 3. it came out of Palette's renderer
unzip -p cuga_workspace/*/deck/deck.pptx ppt/slides/slide1.xml | grep -c "IBM Plex"

Read the thread ids, not the line count. One id carrying both a draft_async and a build_async is a healthy run. Several ids with no build is the signature failure.

The docs are tested too

Every make target a doc tells you to run must exist; every relative link must resolve; every from palette_skill import … a doc prints is actually executed; cross-references to SKILL.md headings must resolve; reversed guidance is banned by string; and exactly one document may carry a runnable start-to-deck sequence.

07Failures worth knowing

Every one was an accurate instruction that was not followable.

These are recorded because they explain why the skill is shaped the way it is. None was caught by a test; each was found by running the thing and reading the server log.

What happenedWhy it read as reasonableThe structural fix
Agent announced a finished deck. Server log: four draft_async calls, zero builds. Each retry started a fresh draft and orphaned the previous session. Nothing in the transcript looked wrong. run_deck owns the thread id; completion is computed by stat-ing files, not asserted.
Agent stopped mid-build: "let me know if you'd like me to keep checking." Asking permission is polite. But prose with no code reads as a final answer, and the build finished uncollected. Every turn between start and done must contain a deck call; the preset enables auto-continue.
Agent gave up at step 39 of 100 while the build was still running. A 25s poll made a ten-minute build cost ~24 steps. The agent ran out of patience, not budget. poll_seconds per host, sized to that host's step budget; a test keeps them matched.
Agent paused for approval that had already been given. The docs said "draft, show me, then build it" should pause — but that phrasing carries its own permission. --pause-after-plan is for an explicit gate only; the distinction is pinned by a test.
Installing for Claude Code silently re-rendered the checkout for Claude Code. payload/ holds one host at a time; the install path never restored it. make skill-check then failed for no visible reason. install() snapshots and restores, exactly as check() already did.
User could not find a deck the agent had genuinely built. "pptx": "deck/deck.pptx" is correct inside the sandbox and useless outside it. pptx_path and dir are absolute, and dir is returned from the first call.
The pattern. Prose cannot fix a behaviour the model has a reason to prefer. Three escalating instructions failed to stop a false completion; what stopped it was moving the claim out of prose entirely and into a flag the tool computes. The same lesson applies to the next field: an instruction read thirty thousand tokens ago competes with the pull toward summarising, so the next command now travels in the output the agent just printed.

08Which doc is for what

Split by what you are trying to do — so a command appears in exactly one of them.

palette_skill/CHEATSHEET.md You want to do something now. Every runnable command: five reset levels from "nothing" to a full two-repo nuke, build, release, install, run, verify — plus a symptom → fix table. §0 is the whole loop in six lines.
palette_skill/GUIDE.md You are changing the skill. What a skill is, the architecture diagram, what each make target produces, when to cut a release, and how remote deployments differ.
palette_skill/TESTING.md You want to trust it. The nine tiers in full, what each failure looks like on the wire, and an honest list of what none of it catches.
palette_skill/README.md You are reading the code. Why the client is shaped this way, and a module-by-module layout.
palette_skill/payload/SKILL.md You want to know what the agent is told. The instructions themselves. Largely generated — read it rather than editing inside the fenced regions.
palette_skill/payload/reference.md You are calling the client from Python. Full signatures, run_deck's state machine, error types, the CLI surface.
README.md You want to run Palette itself. Install, the web UI, config, containers, deployment — and the doc map this page mirrors.
cuga-agent/tests/e2e/skills/README.md You are running the deck tests. The CUGA side: what the three routes assert and why the bare-request one is deliberately unscaffolded.

Source worth reading

  • contract.py — every endpoint, written once. The client, the docs and the tests all read it.
  • hosts.py — the host profiles. The only host-specific part of the whole skill.
  • client.py — PaletteClient and run_deck's resumable state machine.
  • build_skill.py — the region renderers.
  • release.py — artifact assembly and the release guards.
  • Makefile — every target, with make help as the menu.
Palette is IBM/project-palette on the palette_skill branch; the CUGA integration is cuga-project/cuga-agent on palette. All file links above point at those branches. Start at the cheatsheet — it is the only doc that tells you what to type.
